Register Paper locations have been assigned, authors can now register: Author Registration Information Paper presentation preferences emails to Authors have been sent, responses are due by Sept. 30 AOE The Career site is open See this blog post for details on the registration process Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. Santos University of Amsterdam Mission Statement The Neural Information Processing Systems Foundation is a non-profit corporation whose purpose is to foster the exchange of research advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, principally by hosting an annual interdisciplinary academic conference with the highest ethical standards for a diverse and inclusive community. About the Conference The conference was founded in 1987 and is now a multi-track interdisciplinary annual meeting that includes invited talks, demonstrations, symposia, and oral and poster presentations of refereed papers. Along with the conference is a professional exposition focusing on machine learning in practice, a series of tutorials, and topical workshops that provide a less formal setting for the exchange of ideas. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: Submission quotas and reciprocal reviewing The number of submissions to ICML keeps growing faster than the number of qualified reviewers. To keep the review process fair and informative for all authors, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens its reciprocal reviewing requirement. These rules are similar to those adopted by ICLR 2027. Submission quotas No author may appear as a co-author on more than 20 submissions. Each author may appear as a co-author on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer (see below). In plain terms: if neither you nor any of your co-authors has published at one of the venues listed below, you may submit at most one paper to ICML 2027. We welcome submissions from researchers who are new to the field, and these submissions are reviewed like all others. Quotas are checked when abstracts are registered. Authors who exceed a quota will be notified and can fix the problem before the full paper deadline (January 22, 2027). If a quota is still exceeded at the full paper deadline, the program chairs will desk reject excess submissions at random until every author is within the quotas. Who is an eligible reciprocal reviewer An author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer if they have at least one paper accepted at one of the following venues by the abstract registration deadline (January 14, 2027): ICML, NeurIPS, ICLR, UAI, AISTATS, JMLR, TMLR (including Datasets and Benchmarks tracks), ACL, EMNLP, EACL, NAACL, IJCNLP-AACL, Computational Linguistics, TACL (including Findings), COLM CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, TPAMI, AAAI, IJCAI, JAIR, 3DV ICRA, IROS, RSS, CoRL KDD COLT Other publications associated with these venues do not count. This includes workshop papers, position papers, short papers, system demonstrations, industry papers and blog posts. Eligibility is determined from OpenReview profiles, so all authors must keep their profiles complete and up to date, including their publications or DBLP link. Incorrect profile information may lead to desk rejection. Reciprocal reviewing requirement Per-submission requirement: each submission must designate one of its authors as its reciprocal reviewer when the abstract is registered. The designated author must: be an eligible reciprocal reviewer; register as a reviewer for ICML 2027; complete their assigned reviews during the reviewing period (February 24–March 16, 2027). An author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Submissions in which no author is eligible are exempt from this requirement, but they count toward the one-submission quota above. Per-author requirement: authors with 3 or more submissions must serve on the program committee of ICML 2027, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Authors who serve as area chairs, senior area chairs or members of the organizing committee meet this requirement through that role. Responsibilities and enforcement Reciprocal reviewers have the same obligations as all other reviewers. They must follow the reviewing guidelines and the LLM policy, submit their reviews on time, and take part in the discussion with authors and area chairs. The program chairs may desk reject the submissions for which an author is the designated reciprocal reviewer if that author: does not submit their reviews; submits reviews of very low quality;. Submissions that do not designate an eligible reciprocal reviewer when one is available among their authors may also be desk rejected.

It also protects you: the official portal is the only guaranteed way to access approved hotels at conference rates, rather than risking a fraudulent or unauthorized site. Venue Venue information will be posted here The conference is a five-day multi-track event with a mix of invited talks, oral paper presentations, and poster sessions. The fourth and fifth day are workshops. Book your room (December) Exhibitors We thank our exhibitors for all their support! Information on becoming an exhibitor will be posted here. View Exhibitors Contact Us Exhibitor Info » Important Dates Abstract Deadline Sep 18 '26 (Anywhere on Earth) Paper Deadline Sep 25 '26 (Anywhere on Earth) Reviews Released Nov 05 '26 * Final Decisions Dec 16 '26 * View All Dates Time zone: Conference local time zone About the Conference The International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) is the premier gathering of professionals dedicated to the advancement of the branch of artificial intelligence called representation learning, but generally referred to as deep learning. ICLR is globally renowned for presenting and publishing cutting-edge research on all aspects of deep learning used in the fields of artificial intelligence, statistics and data science, as well as important application areas such as machine vision, computational biology, speech recognition, text understanding, gaming, and robotics. ICLR is one of the fastest growing artificial intelligence conferences in the world. Participants at ICLR span a wide range of backgrounds, from academic and industrial researchers, to entrepreneurs and engineers, to graduate students and postdocs. The rapidly developing field of deep learning is concerned with questions surrounding how we can best learn meaningful and useful representations of data. items.content: Featured projects TL;DR Helion now uses compile-time heuristics that analyze a kernel’s IR and dataflow to pick fast settings without slow autotuning. It classifies the kernel as matmul, reduction, or pointwise and chooses block sizes, warps, and stages, giving near-autotuned speed for free. Introduction Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning . We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write. Highlights: Autotuner Heuristics. Our heuristics cover a large set of kernels, including GEMM, reductions, and even linear attention. Linear attention. Over 96 kernel-and-shape cells spanning nine linear-attention variants, the computed config beats the hand-written Triton in Flash Linear Attention (FLA) by 1.18x in the forward pass, and by 1.12x with backward included on H100. Overall the heuristic is 2.13x faster than Helion’s previous no-autotune default on H100. vLLM reduction kernels. Over 153 kernel-and-shape cells across six production kernels on H100, the computed config is 1.27x faster than vLLM’s own handwritten CUDA/C++ operators, and 2.2x faster than Helion’s previous default. The analysis itself is cheap. Compiling a kernel with the heuristics on versus off differs negligibly (tens of milliseconds), which is lost in the noise of Triton compilation. Our Approach: Decide the Config at Compile Time A single Helion kernel can lower into thousands of different Triton kernels. One definition covers block sizes, loop orders, indexing modes and pipelining strategies, but the autotuner has to choose which of those thousands to emit, by compiling and benchmarking many candidates. And this autotuning cost is per kernel and per shape , which multiplies the problem the more kernels, shapes, and hardware backends you want to support. We compute the config at compile time instead of searching for it at tuning time. We read the device IR and record structural facts about it: which axes are tiled, which block sizes are tunable, which tiles are live at which part of the kernel, etc. A heuristic reads those facts and emits a config. The point here is not to come up with a better config than the autotuner, which has the benefit of benchmarking potentially thousands of configs before selecting one. It is to add a point in the tradeoff space between performance and wait time. Our heuristics serve two purposes. A primary heuristic emits the default config used when autotuning is disabled. When autotuning is enabled, helper heuristics generate roughly 5–20 related or alternative configs that seed the autotuner. The goals are different: the default config should perform well on its own, while the seeds should give the autotuner several promising starting points to speed up autotuning. In this blog, we’ll touch on both, but focus on the primary heuristic that gets emitted with autotuning off. How the Heuristics Work A heuristic sets the values for various config knobs, which must be tuned carefully to achieve high performance and are normally picked by the autotuner. These include block sizes for each tiled axis, num_warps, num_stages, the L2 grouping, load eviction policies, and more. We pick a heuristic by scanning the device IR for the operations a kernel contains. Any matmul routes to the matmul heuristic regardless of what else is in the kernel; a reduction with no matmul routes to the reduction heuristic; everything else receives the pointwise heuristic. If a kernel’s extents are not all known at compile time, no heuristic fires and Helion falls back to the original default. Our heuristics all lean on the same underlying analysis, which estimates resource usage of the kernel. At any step of the kernel, the analysis determines: given a candidate set of block sizes, how many registers, shared memory, and — on Blackwell — how much tensor memory, one CTA needs at that moment. To do this, we run a liveness analysis on the compiler IR and walk each graph to find where every value is last used, and guess where it will be placed in memory. This is a hard problem: we are trying to predict what Triton will keep in registers, what it will stage through shared memory, what it will materialize at all rather than fuse away. Sometimes it is easier to predict (e.g., we assume the output of an hl.dot will be placed in TMEM on B200), but the estimate is approximate. Using this we can estimate things that matter for performance, such as: Occupancy : how many CTAs fit on an SM at once. Whichever space runs out first decides it, e.g., a CTA needing a tenth of the SM’s registers and a tenth of its shared memory, but six tenths of its tensor memory, gets one CTA per SM, since two CTAs would go over the tensor memory budget by 20% (0.6 x 2 = 1.2). Register pressure: Peak live registers spread over the threads we intend to launch tells us whether the assembler will be forced to spill. These considerations inform the selection of different config knobs. We’ll illustrate this for the matmul heuristic : block_size: If the launch produces fewer CTAs than the GPU has SMs, we shrink block size on a grid axis to produce more of them. num_stages: More stages hide more load latency, so we want as many as shared memory allows. But stages can also accidentally lose occupancy: six of them might fit while eating the CTA’s entire shared-memory budget, leaving one CTA per SM, where three stages and two CTAs per SM is the better trade. num_warps. Two things pull on this: Which instruction Triton emits. Below four warps, or with an M block under 64, Triton uses the smaller synchronous MMA; otherwise it uses the big high-throughput one (wgmma on Hopper, tcgen05 on Blackwell). Usually we want the big one. But when there is little matmul work sometimes the better answer is many CTAs per SM running small MMAs that overlap each other’s loads. So we count dynamic matmul work (essentially counting the number of times the hl.dot will be executed dynamically) and choose based on that. Register pressure. Warps divide the tile across more threads, so more warps means less pressure on each one. If the peak live state at the current count would spill, that argues for increasing warps. Feasibility Check. A final pessimistic pass over the whole kernel: add up tensor memory, shared memory and registers, and confirm the config can actually launch. The adjustments above already respect these budgets, so this is mostly defensive. In the case where there are multiple matmuls in one kernel (for example for attention and linear attention), we run the matmul heuristic on each hl.dot and use those as the starting point. They may disagree: two dots can share one block-size knob — one dot’s N is frequently the next dot’s K — and there is only one num_warps for the whole kernel. To resolve these tradeoffs, we rank each dot by estimated importance: priority goes to any dot with a loop-carried accumulator, since that accumulator stays resident for the whole loop and its tile sets the kernel’s footprint; then its dynamic matmul work; then its own output area. Wherever two dots disagree about a knob, the higher-ranked one wins (for example num_warps is set by the top-ranked dot alone). The reduction heuristic works through a similar set of knobs: num_warps. Three pressures here, pulling in different directions: Enough warps to do the reduction. A wide reduction needs warps working on it, so a ladder off the largest selected reduction sets the starting point: 128 elements wants one or two warps, 16,384 wants many more. Residency. More warps per CTA means fewer CTAs per SM (there is a per-SM CTA limit), so we also test fewer warps. Register pressure. Adjust warps to not spill registers. block_size. Fitting more CTAs per SM means potentially smaller tiles, so we shrink blocks back down to buy residency. The constraint is that an axis with stride 1 is the one carrying the coalesced loads, and shrinking it too far loses load coalescing. Persistence. A reduction can be kept resident and done in one pass, or walked in chunks. The case that matters is a row the kernel reads twice — RMSNorm reads it once to compute the scale and again to apply it — and when we can prove that, staying persistent is allowed to cost some spilling and some residency, because it saves the second trip to memory. Because the warp count depends on the blocks and the blocks depend on the warp count, we iterate until both hold still for a full round (in practice this doesn’t take very long). Result 1: Config Quality, with No Tuning Time Linear attention We measured nine linear-attention variants in forward and forward-plus-backward, over six production shapes, on H100. The six shapes span batch 1 to 8, 8 to 96 heads, sequence 1024 to 16384 and head dimension 64 to 256. The baseline is Flash Linear Attention (FLA), an open-source, widely used library of hand-written Triton kernels. The autotuned arm in the charts (“Helion AOT config”) is the result of running the full autotuner once per shape and saving the winner — how you would ship a Helion kernel for a known set of shapes today. Before this work the choice was binary: take Helion’s no-autotune default and run at 0.52x of handwritten FLA Triton, or spend GPU-hours autotuning and reach 1.26x . The heuristic adds a third option that did not exist before: 1.18x , with no autotuning price (most of what autotuning finds, available immediately) and it moves Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior from losing to handwritten Triton to beating it, at least for this set of kernels. vLLM’s reduction kernels vLLM is a widely deployed open-source LLM inference engine, and it ships its own hand-written CUDA/C++ kernels for the operations on its serving hot path. There are six reduction kernels — two FP8 quantizers, RMSNorm and SiLU-and-multiply each fused with quantization, and fused QK-normalization plus RoPE– for which vLLM already had Helion implementations, contributed by the team behind an earlier post in this series . That makes them a good test: production kernels, written by someone else, against the hand-written CUDA they were meant to replace. And we get a similar result, in a different codebase. Helion’s no-autotune default runs at 0.58x of vLLM’s CUDA; the computed config reaches 1.27x ; full autotuning gets to 1.31x . The interesting number is the last gap: on these kernels autotuning buys only about 3% over the config we compute for free. The everyday kernels, against torch.compile Both comparisons above are specialist libraries — linear-attention variants and FP8 quantizers. This one is deliberately the opposite: the kernels everybody writes. RMSNorm, LayerNorm, softmax, cross entropy and friends, similar to the suite the introduction post benchmarked when it first measured Helion. Most of the kernels benchmarked in this section can be found here . The reference baseline here is torch.compile(mode=”max-autotune-no-cudagraphs”): we force torch.compile onto its Triton backend so we are not comparing against handwritten libraries (e.g.. cuBLAS) but instead against generated Triton from a widely-used compiler. There is no tuned-config arm in this section, for the mundane reason that we do not have full autotune runs for these kernels (which would take many GPU hours to produce). On a suite of ten reduction kernels and 80 (kernel, shape) combinations, the computed config comes out at 1.09x of max-autotune torch.compile, with no tuning of its own. Helion’s unseeded default is 0.27x . We also sweep across thirteen matmul kernel families over 70 shapes. The computed config comes out at 1.88x of max-autotune torch.compile overall, against 0.51x for Helion’s default. Two caveats on that 1.88x. The comparisons are not always apples-to-apples – for some of these kernels the PyTorch implementation materializes intermediates that the Helion kernel fuses. And jagged HSTU attention is a genuine regression: the old default happens to land on a good config there (3.72x) and the heuristic does worse (3.27x). Result 2: Does the Seed Make the Search Faster? Everything above is about the config Helion emits when autotuning is off . But the same configs can be handed to the autotuner as its starting population, and in principle a good starting point should let the search finish sooner. In addition to this primary config, the helper heuristics also add somewhere between 5 and 20 new variations / approaches. To test it we took 38 matmul and multi-matmul kernels — linear attention, attention, Mamba, and other wild cards like squeeze-and-excitation — and one shape for each kernel. Then we ran the full autotune effort on every cell twice: once from random configs, once with the compiler’s seeds in the initial population. The short answer from this run is that seeding buys a lot early but much less late . Here is one cell, chosen as a clear example of the pattern. The x-axis tracks the number of configs tried, while the y-axis tracks performance relative to the best config we found. Seeded, the first config is far superior to the unseeded first config. But unseeded quickly catches up, and they end up sitting on the same answer while the search grinds through several hundred more configs. The early advantage is enormous while the final advantage is zero. That is the pattern across all 38 cells. Medians below; counts include configs that failed to compile or failed to produce a timing, since those consume budget too. Search target Median configs (no seeds / seeded) within 50% of the best found 35.5 / 1.0 within 25% 103.5 / 2.5 within 5% 255.5 / 175.0 complete search 521.5 / 420.5 The advantage is concentrated entirely at the start: 35x fewer configs to reach something merely decent, 41x to get within 25%, but only 1.5x to get within 5% and 1.2x to finish the search. One thing this result is not: seeding does not make the final config any better. Replaying both arms’ winners on one GPU, they land within a fraction of a percent of each other. This is about how long the search takes, not where it ends up. Limitations and Future Work A central limitation is that these heuristics predict what another compiler will do. Every budget depends on guessing where a value ends up — registers, shared memory, or tensor memory — and that is Triton’s decision, not ours. Some of it is safe to bet on: on B200 a matmul result is going to be in tensor memory. Plenty of it we get wrong. There are several possible directions of future work. Measure instead of predicting. The cleanest fix for the limitation above is to stop guessing: compile once, read the register and shared-memory usage the assembler reported, and correct the estimate from there. Fire on more kernels. We currently decline whenever we lack the information to size anything — a loop tiled over a range only known at runtime, for instance. A less-educated guess would be easy: a default extent, a mean, something. Configs would be worse without that information, but the alternative today is the base default, which the results above show is very bad — so the guess is probably still worth making. Touch more knobs. We set block sizes, num_warps and num_stages, plus some L2 grouping and L2 eviction policy. That leaves a long list untouched — tensor descriptors versus pointer arithmetic, persistent versus flat launch, etc. Individually these are probably worth less than the ones we do set, but there is certainly performance left on the table. Specialize the heuristics. They are deliberately general: one multi-matmul heuristic has to do well on attention and linear attention, one reduction heuristic on RMSNorm and vLLM’s quantization kernels. An alternative is parent heuristics with children — a vLLMQuantizationHeuristic that starts from ReductionHeuristic’s answer and then specializes on what it knows about that family. Other backends. Everything here is evaluated on NVIDIA, and the heuristics ship enabled for H100 and B200 on the Triton backend. Nothing in the approach is NVIDIA-specific — the analysis is parameterized by hardware limits that should apply across backends — but the constants and ladders were tuned against these two chips. Conclusion These heuristics are merged into Helion and enabled by default on H100 and B200 with the Triton backend. If you would like to learn more, please check out the autotuner heuristics . The point is not that static analysis beats search, but rather that the gap is now small enough that skipping the search is a reasonable thing to do for some kernels. Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior went from 0.52x handwritten FLA Triton to 1.18x, and from 0.58x vLLM’s handwritten CUDA to 1.27x, with nothing compiled and nothing benchmarked. On a general suite of reduction kernels it sits at 1.09x torch.compile max-autotune. Full autotuning remains the right call when you are shipping a fixed set of shapes and can pay for it once; what changed is that the alternative is no longer a large concession.

The goals are different: the default config should perform well on its own, while the seeds should give the autotuner several promising starting points to speed up autotuning. In this blog, we’ll touch on both, but focus on the primary heuristic that gets emitted with autotuning off. How the Heuristics Work A heuristic sets the values for various config knobs, which must be tuned carefully to achieve high performance and are normally picked by the autotuner. These include block sizes for each tiled axis, num_warps, num_stages, the L2 grouping, load eviction policies, and more. We pick a heuristic by scanning the device IR for the operations a kernel contains. Any matmul routes to the matmul heuristic regardless of what else is in the kernel; a reduction with no matmul routes to the reduction heuristic; everything else receives the pointwise heuristic. If a kernel’s extents are not all known at compile time, no heuristic fires and Helion falls back to the original default. Our heuristics all lean on the same underlying analysis, which estimates resource usage of the kernel. At any step of the kernel, the analysis determines: given a candidate set of block sizes, how many registers, shared memory, and — on Blackwell — how much tensor memory, one CTA needs at that moment. To do this, we run a liveness analysis on the compiler IR and walk each graph to find where every value is last used, and guess where it will be placed in memory. This is a hard problem: we are trying to predict what Triton will keep in registers, what it will stage through shared memory, what it will materialize at all rather than fuse away. Sometimes it is easier to predict (e.g., we assume the output of an hl.dot will be placed in TMEM on B200), but the estimate is approximate. Using this we can estimate things that matter for performance, such as: Occupancy : how many CTAs fit on an SM at once. Whichever space runs out first decides it, e.g., a CTA needing a tenth of the SM’s registers and a tenth of its shared memory, but six tenths of its tensor memory, gets one CTA per SM, since two CTAs would go over the tensor memory budget by 20% (0.6 x 2 = 1.2). Register pressure: Peak live registers spread over the threads we intend to launch tells us whether the assembler will be forced to spill. These considerations inform the selection of different config knobs. We’ll illustrate this for the matmul heuristic : block_size: If the launch produces fewer CTAs than the GPU has SMs, we shrink block size on a grid axis to produce more of them. num_stages: More stages hide more load latency, so we want as many as shared memory allows. But stages can also accidentally lose occupancy: six of them might fit while eating the CTA’s entire shared-memory budget, leaving one CTA per SM, where three stages and two CTAs per SM is the better trade. num_warps. Two things pull on this: Which instruction Triton emits. Below four warps, or with an M block under 64, Triton uses the smaller synchronous MMA; otherwise it uses the big high-throughput one (wgmma on Hopper, tcgen05 on Blackwell). Usually we want the big one. But when there is little matmul work sometimes the better answer is many CTAs per SM running small MMAs that overlap each other’s loads. So we count dynamic matmul work (essentially counting the number of times the hl.dot will be executed dynamically) and choose based on that. Register pressure. Warps divide the tile across more threads, so more warps means less pressure on each one. If the peak live state at the current count would spill, that argues for increasing warps. Feasibility Check. A final pessimistic pass over the whole kernel: add up tensor memory, shared memory and registers, and confirm the config can actually launch. The adjustments above already respect these budgets, so this is mostly defensive. In the case where there are multiple matmuls in one kernel (for example for attention and linear attention), we run the matmul heuristic on each hl.dot and use those as the starting point. They may disagree: two dots can share one block-size knob — one dot’s N is frequently the next dot’s K — and there is only one num_warps for the whole kernel. To resolve these tradeoffs, we rank each dot by estimated importance: priority goes to any dot with a loop-carried accumulator, since that accumulator stays resident for the whole loop and its tile sets the kernel’s footprint; then its dynamic matmul work; then its own output area. Wherever two dots disagree about a knob, the higher-ranked one wins (for example num_warps is set by the top-ranked dot alone). The reduction heuristic works through a similar set of knobs: num_warps. Three pressures here, pulling in different directions: Enough warps to do the reduction. A wide reduction needs warps working on it, so a ladder off the largest selected reduction sets the starting point: 128 elements wants one or two warps, 16,384 wants many more. Residency. More warps per CTA means fewer CTAs per SM (there is a per-SM CTA limit), so we also test fewer warps. Register pressure. Adjust warps to not spill registers. block_size. Fitting more CTAs per SM means potentially smaller tiles, so we shrink blocks back down to buy residency. The constraint is that an axis with stride 1 is the one carrying the coalesced loads, and shrinking it too far loses load coalescing. Persistence. A reduction can be kept resident and done in one pass, or walked in chunks. The case that matters is a row the kernel reads twice — RMSNorm reads it once to compute the scale and again to apply it — and when we can prove that, staying persistent is allowed to cost some spilling and some residency, because it saves the second trip to memory. Because the warp count depends on the blocks and the blocks depend on the warp count, we iterate until both hold still for a full round (in practice this doesn’t take very long). Result 1: Config Quality, with No Tuning Time Linear attention We measured nine linear-attention variants in forward and forward-plus-backward, over six production shapes, on H100. The six shapes span batch 1 to 8, 8 to 96 heads, sequence 1024 to 16384 and head dimension 64 to 256. The baseline is Flash Linear Attention (FLA), an open-source, widely used library of hand-written Triton kernels. The autotuned arm in the charts (“Helion AOT config”) is the result of running the full autotuner once per shape and saving the winner — how you would ship a Helion kernel for a known set of shapes today. Before this work the choice was binary: take Helion’s no-autotune default and run at 0.52x of handwritten FLA Triton, or spend GPU-hours autotuning and reach 1.26x . The heuristic adds a third option that did not exist before: 1.18x , with no autotuning price (most of what autotuning finds, available immediately) and it moves Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior from losing to handwritten Triton to beating it, at least for this set of kernels. vLLM’s reduction kernels vLLM is a widely deployed open-source LLM inference engine, and it ships its own hand-written CUDA/C++ kernels for the operations on its serving hot path. There are six reduction kernels — two FP8 quantizers, RMSNorm and SiLU-and-multiply each fused with quantization, and fused QK-normalization plus RoPE– for which vLLM already had Helion implementations, contributed by the team behind an earlier post in this series . That makes them a good test: production kernels, written by someone else, against the hand-written CUDA they were meant to replace. And we get a similar result, in a different codebase. Helion’s no-autotune default runs at 0.58x of vLLM’s CUDA; the computed config reaches 1.27x ; full autotuning gets to 1.31x . The interesting number is the last gap: on these kernels autotuning buys only about 3% over the config we compute for free. The everyday kernels, against torch.compile Both comparisons above are specialist libraries — linear-attention variants and FP8 quantizers. This one is deliberately the opposite: the kernels everybody writes. RMSNorm, LayerNorm, softmax, cross entropy and friends, similar to the suite the introduction post benchmarked when it first measured Helion. Most of the kernels benchmarked in this section can be found here . The reference baseline here is torch.compile(mode=”max-autotune-no-cudagraphs”): we force torch.compile onto its Triton backend so we are not comparing against handwritten libraries (e.g.. cuBLAS) but instead against generated Triton from a widely-used compiler. There is no tuned-config arm in this section, for the mundane reason that we do not have full autotune runs for these kernels (which would take many GPU hours to produce). On a suite of ten reduction kernels and 80 (kernel, shape) combinations, the computed config comes out at 1.09x of max-autotune torch.compile, with no tuning of its own. Helion’s unseeded default is 0.27x . We also sweep across thirteen matmul kernel families over 70 shapes. The computed config comes out at 1.88x of max-autotune torch.compile overall, against 0.51x for Helion’s default. Two caveats on that 1.88x. The comparisons are not always apples-to-apples – for some of these kernels the PyTorch implementation materializes intermediates that the Helion kernel fuses. And jagged HSTU attention is a genuine regression: the old default happens to land on a good config there (3.72x) and the heuristic does worse (3.27x). Result 2: Does the Seed Make the Search Faster? Everything above is about the config Helion emits when autotuning is off . But the same configs can be handed to the autotuner as its starting population, and in principle a good starting point should let the search finish sooner. In addition to this primary config, the helper heuristics also add somewhere between 5 and 20 new variations / approaches. To test it we took 38 matmul and multi-matmul kernels — linear attention, attention, Mamba, and other wild cards like squeeze-and-excitation — and one shape for each kernel. Then we ran the full autotune effort on every cell twice: once from random configs, once with the compiler’s seeds in the initial population. The short answer from this run is that seeding buys a lot early but much less late . Here is one cell, chosen as a clear example of the pattern. The x-axis tracks the number of configs tried, while the y-axis tracks performance relative to the best config we found. Seeded, the first config is far superior to the unseeded first config. But unseeded quickly catches up, and they end up sitting on the same answer while the search grinds through several hundred more configs. The early advantage is enormous while the final advantage is zero. That is the pattern across all 38 cells. Medians below; counts include configs that failed to compile or failed to produce a timing, since those consume budget too. Search target Median configs (no seeds / seeded) within 50% of the best found 35.5 / 1.0 within 25% 103.5 / 2.5 within 5% 255.5 / 175.0 complete search 521.5 / 420.5 The advantage is concentrated entirely at the start: 35x fewer configs to reach something merely decent, 41x to get within 25%, but only 1.5x to get within 5% and 1.2x to finish the search. One thing this result is not: seeding does not make the final config any better. Replaying both arms’ winners on one GPU, they land within a fraction of a percent of each other. This is about how long the search takes, not where it ends up. Limitations and Future Work A central limitation is that these heuristics predict what another compiler will do. Every budget depends on guessing where a value ends up — registers, shared memory, or tensor memory — and that is Triton’s decision, not ours. Some of it is safe to bet on: on B200 a matmul result is going to be in tensor memory. Plenty of it we get wrong. There are several possible directions of future work. Measure instead of predicting. The cleanest fix for the limitation above is to stop guessing: compile once, read the register and shared-memory usage the assembler reported, and correct the estimate from there. Fire on more kernels. We currently decline whenever we lack the information to size anything — a loop tiled over a range only known at runtime, for instance. A less-educated guess would be easy: a default extent, a mean, something. Configs would be worse without that information, but the alternative today is the base default, which the results above show is very bad — so the guess is probably still worth making. Touch more knobs. We set block sizes, num_warps and num_stages, plus some L2 grouping and L2 eviction policy. That leaves a long list untouched — tensor descriptors versus pointer arithmetic, persistent versus flat launch, etc. Individually these are probably worth less than the ones we do set, but there is certainly performance left on the table. Specialize the heuristics. They are deliberately general: one multi-matmul heuristic has to do well on attention and linear attention, one reduction heuristic on RMSNorm and vLLM’s quantization kernels. An alternative is parent heuristics with children — a vLLMQuantizationHeuristic that starts from ReductionHeuristic’s answer and then specializes on what it knows about that family. Other backends. Everything here is evaluated on NVIDIA, and the heuristics ship enabled for H100 and B200 on the Triton backend. Nothing in the approach is NVIDIA-specific — the analysis is parameterized by hardware limits that should apply across backends — but the constants and ladders were tuned against these two chips. Conclusion These heuristics are merged into Helion and enabled by default on H100 and B200 with the Triton backend. If you would like to learn more, please check out the autotuner heuristics . The point is not that static analysis beats search, but rather that the gap is now small enough that skipping the search is a reasonable thing to do for some kernels. Helion’s out-of-the-box behavior went from 0.52x handwritten FLA Triton to 1.18x, and from 0.58x vLLM’s handwritten CUDA to 1.27x, with nothing compiled and nothing benchmarked. On a general suite of reduction kernels it sits at 1.09x torch.compile max-autotune. Full autotuning remains the right call when you are shipping a fixed set of shapes and can pay for it once; what changed is that the alternative is no longer a large concession.

items.content: KEY DATES We invite submissions for workshop proposals for the 7th Multidisciplinary Conference on Reinforcement Learning and Decision Making (RLDM2027), to be held July 6-9, 2027 at Maison de la Chimie, Paris, France. Workshops are a half-day and held during the conference. Submissions due : January 8, 2027, 23:59 UTC Decisions announced : by February 14, 2027 Conference : 6–9 July 2027 WHAT ARE RLDM WORKSHOPS? The goal of the RLDM workshops is to encourage interdisciplinary discussion and to provide an informal forum for researchers to discuss important questions and challenges focused on a specific topic. Workshop topics may include anything from important current/controversial issues, open problems, and comparisons of competing approaches. You are free to choose a format that suits the topic, and in the past have included invited oral presentations,’blitz’ talks, panel discussions, data modeling challenges, hackathons, debates, and symposia aimed at improving communication between researchers from different fields rather than presenting novel research. Or a combination of any of those! Workshop organizers propose the workshop content, coordinate speakers, and provide the program for the workshop in a timely manner (a rough suggested timeline will be posted in the FAQ soon). Organizing a workshop is your chance to shape the conference or kickstart a new community, so we encourage researchers at all stages of their career to consider getting involved in a workshop proposal. For inspiration, have a look here for workshops at RLDM2025: https://rldm.org/past-meetings/rldm2025/workshops/ HOW TO SUBMIT Workshop proposals are due by 23:59 UTC on Friday, January 8, 2027 . They should be submitted using this form . Notifications will be provided by email on or before February 14, 2027 . Proposals will be asked to respond to the following questions: – Workshop title and acronym (if available). – A brief description of the workshop focus (max 2000 characters). – A brief justification of how this workshop engages the multidisciplinary RLDM community . If a similar theme has been explored in recent years or at other venues, please highlight the new developments that warrant revisiting this topic (max 1000 characters). – A short description of the format of planned activities (talks, panels, invited speakers, activities, etc.) (max 1500 characters), – A list of invited speakers , and indicate who has confirmed their willingness to participate. Note that it is not necessary at this stage to have established confirmation from all participants in the workshop and that the workshops are 1/2 day. – A list of workshop organizers with web page URLs if available. – A brief mention of any past event or workshop organizing experience . We encourage at least one organizer to have past event organizing experience. (max 500 characters) -The email addresses of all workshop co-organizers . FAQ Is there any travel funding available for workshop speakers? RLDM will not be able to provide travel funding for workshop speakers. In previous years, some workshops have sought and received funding from external sources to bring in outside speakers and RLDM is open to that model. Organizers should list all funding sources in the proposal. Who should I contact with questions? Please feel free to contact us at rebitz@gmail.com and giorgia.ramponi@uzh.ch if you have any questions! For the quickest response please use “RLDM2027 Workshops” in your subject line. How will proposals be evaluated? Workshop proposals will be evaluated and selected by the RLDM Workshop Chairs based on the following metrics, in no particular order: – Relevance to the RLDM community; – Interdisciplinary scope of the proposal; – Current interest in the topic within the community; – Diversity and equity in the proposed presenters/speakers/organizers; – Potential for new research directions and interactions to emerge. What if I want to get involved with a workshop proposal, but I don’t have co-organizers? Please get in touch with us over email; we might be able to pair you with other possible co-organizers. How many workshops will there be? Around five.

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. Opens in a new tab Meet the authors Chenglong Wang Principal Researcher Learn more Yuwei Xiao Computer Science Ph.D. Student UCLA Learn more Alper Sarikaya Senior Data Visualization Engineer Power BI Learn more Michel Galley Senior Principal Research Manager Learn more Chris Quirk Partner Researcher Learn more Jianfeng Gao Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President Learn more Research Areas Artificial intelligence Research Groups Deep Learning Group Related labs Microsoft Research Redmond

Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary.
