items.content: Featured projects TL;DR Scaling pretraining for a ~1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model on shared, public infrastructure was previously considered unfeasible due to unique architectural and interconnect bottlenecks. However, by leveraging the fine-grained flexibility of PyTorch and TorchTitan, the EUROPA consortium successfully unlocked frontier-scale training on JUPITER, boosting throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/sec per GPU across 384 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs per DP replica (96 nodes) as part of the EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge. The EuroHPC Frontier AI Grand Challenge was designed to prove that sovereign, open-source AI could compete at frontier levels using shared public resources. As part of that process, we – as the EUROPA consortium, formed by Domyn and Fraunhofer IAIS and IIS – were selected to an open European Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model of at least 400B parameters, support for all 24 official EU languages, and strict compliance with the EU AI Act. In this post, we describe how we scaled pretraining to 1T MoE on JUPITER , the EuroHPC exascale supercomputer hosted at Forschungszentrum Jülich, proving that public infrastructure can indeed sustain frontier scale. Total parameters 951.9B (32.8B active per token) Layers 74 Hidden size 6,144 Experts 384 routed, top-8 Expert hidden size 1,792 Vocabulary 256,000 Pretrain Sequence length 65,536 tokens Optimizer Muon + AdamW The table lists the configuration used for the experiments in the post. Models of this size are usually trained on clusters that their developers operate or rent for exclusive use. JUPITER is instead publicly funded research infrastructure shared by hundreds of projects. It was also designed to support scientific research at large, which led to architectural choices that are somewhat atypical in the AI space, as we’ll describe in detail later in the post. As such, reaching the 1T parameter scale while maintaining viable throughput requires careful optimizations that go beyond standard distributed techniques. In order to have access to the necessary level of flexibility to perform fine-grained optimizations to the pre-training setup, we chose to go with PyTorch and TorchTitan . Under these conditions, we raised throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200 GPUs (96 nodes). We want to share the main milestones that get us there, each of which builds on TorchTitan’s design and led to contributions back to TorchTitan and PyTorch: FlexShard placement for the Muon optimizer, which removes most of the optimizer’s communication. Activation-checkpoint offloading to the Grace CPU. Running FSDP’s all-gather setup on the compute stream ( unshard_async_op ), which frees ~14 GiB of HBM per GPU. The full write-up covers the remaining changes in detail, with interactive figures and profiler traces. The machine and its constraints Each JUPITER Booster node has four NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. Each superchip pairs a Hopper GPU (96 GB HBM3) with a 72-core Grace CPU (120 GB LPDDR5X), connected by a 900 GB/s NVLink-C2C link. GPUs in a node are connected by NVLink 4 at 150 GB/s per direction, and each node has four InfiniBand NDR200 adapters, about 25 GB/s per GPU. Figure 2. Bandwidths within a JUPITER node, drawn to scale. All inter-node traffic leaves through the thin InfiniBand links. In addition to the accelerators, two key parts of the system are also relevant for the design: Inter-node bandwidth. InfiniBand is 36 times slower than the link between a GPU and its own CPU, and distributing a 1T parameter model over hundreds of accelerators requires crossing that boundary continuously during training. Traffic over InfiniBand must therefore aggressively overlap with computation. Host memory capacity. GH200 is available with up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X per Grace, but JUPITER’s compute nodes actually use the 120 GB configuration (as opposed to login nodes which sport 480GB), which favors bandwidth over capacity. After the kernel’s share, about 108 GiB per GPU is usable, and we found that in practice some nodes start jobs with much less. This limits how much state can be moved out of the HBM. These constraints dictate the parallelism layout: 384-way FSDP with 4-way expert parallelism inside each node and no pipeline parallelism. The MoE token all-to-all is hard to overlap, so we kept it on NVLink. Without pipeline parallelism steps tend to be shorter, which has the advantage of providing fast feedback at scale, and fixed costs are amortized via a large batch of 384 sequences of 65,536 tokens (~25M tokens per step). FSDP already provides us with the overlap of the gather of layer n+1 with the compute of layer n , so most of the remaining work goes into making the overlap effective. We achieve this across three dimensions: moving to longer sequences to compute for longer, reducing the bytes transmitted over InfiniBand, and leveraging Grace memory to provide enough total capacity to hold the model, the gradients and the optimizer state. FlexShard: Muon without the communication We use Muon for every weight matrix except the router and embeddings (about 99.5% of the parameters) and AdamW for the rest. Muon requires one fp32 state per parameter, while Adam requires two. Removing the second state is instrumental in making a 65,536-token sequence fit in memory. Muon orthogonalizes each update with a few Newton-Schulz iterations, which operate on the whole matrix. Because FSDP splits every matrix into 384 shards, a simple implementation gathers each matrix on one rank, runs Newton-Schulz there and scatters the result back. On our interconnect, this communication is too expensive. FlexShard , now part of TorchTitan, lets us control which rank owns which parameters. We shard the experts by whole expert, so every rank owns complete expert matrices and runs their Newton-Schulz iterations with no communication at all. The dense matrices, such as the attention projections, are still collected on an owning rank, and each rank processes its own experts while the dense matrices are in transit, so that communication is overlapped. With FSDP’s CPU offload, the optimizer runs on Grace, where the parameters are stored, and Newton-Schulz on 72 Arm cores takes ~35 s per step. We contributed support to TorchTitan for running Newton-Schulz on the GPU while parameters stay offloaded. The optimizer step went from 41.7 s to 2.2 s, and throughput rose from 441 to 597 tokens/s per GPU (+35%). Figure 3. Rank 0’s profiled step from 80 s onward. Top: Newton-Schulz on Grace, with the GPU idle for ~34 s after the backward pass while the CPU computes. Bottom: Newton-Schulz on Hopper, where the optimizer takes a small fraction of the step. Activation offloading to Grace The volume of weights gathered per layer does not depend on the number of tokens in our setup, so a longer sequence increases compute time while not impacting communication. We first stored activations only at layer boundaries and recomputed everything inside a layer during the backward pass. In TorchTitan this is named FullAC. Since GPU was idle for most of the baseline step, the extra compute did not lengthen it. As a result, throughput went from 90 to 370 tokens/s per GPU at 32,768 tokens. At 65,536 tokens, the boundary activations alone take 74 layers × 65,536 tokens × 6,144 × 2 bytes ≈ 55 GiB per GPU, which does not fit in HBM next to the weights. GH200 has a 900 GB/s link to 120 GB of CPU memory, so we decide to offload them. Each boundary activation is copied to Grace after the forward pass produces it, and copied back to Hopper one layer before the backward pass recomputes it. An offloading parameter sets the share of layers that offload, which trades HBM for Grace memory. TorchTitan’s activation-checkpointing wrapper made this change convenient. We contributed the hooks for activation-checkpoint offloading to TorchTitan and built our offloading strategy on top of them. With offload, throughput rose from 370 to 508 tokens/s per GPU (+37%), and the sequence length grew to 49,152 tokens and then, with Muon, to 65,536. Figure 4. Offload schedule, drawn with 16 layers in place of 74. During the forward pass, each boundary activation moves to Grace. During the backward pass, it returns to HBM one layer before its recomputation. De-fragging FSDPs Streams After an upgrade to our software stack, the CUDA caching allocator started retrying allocations on every rank at ~70% memory utilization. At the time of the retries, 25-30 GiB of HBM was free, but the allocator could not use it. After investigating the root cause, we identified it in how FSDP overlaps communication with computation. FSDP uses one compute stream and four side streams, and the allocator keeps a separate pool per stream. Memory freed by a stream can only be reused by that stream. FSDP allocates each buffer on the stream that writes it, and some of our other communication optimizations allocated temporary buffers inside FSDP’s calls, so these buffers also landed on side streams. Replaying the allocator’s event log at peak memory showed the side streams holding 27.3 GiB, of which only 6.4 GiB was in use. The remaining 20.9 GiB was out of reach of the compute stream, which then could not find a 4 GiB block for a MoE buffer. Figure 5. HBM held by each allocator stream’s cache at peak live memory, reconstructed from the allocator’s event trace on rank 0. Solid bars are live tensors, and dashed bars are cached memory that only the owning stream can reuse. Luckily, FSDP2 has a private flag, unshard_async_op , that runs the all-gather setup on the compute stream and lets NCCL run on its internal stream. The gather buffers are then allocated from, and returned to, the compute stream’s pool. We adapted our custom gather to run asynchronously, so the compute stream waits for the network only when it needs the weights. This brought the number of ranks with allocator retries from 384 to zero. Peak reserved memory went from 88.1 to 74.6 GiB, and throughput rose from 996 to 1,210 tokens/s per GPU. We proposed a TorchTitan option to enable the flag. Following the review, unshard_async_op is being moved into a public FSDP API ( PyTorch #202343 ), so other FSDP users can rely on it. Upstreaming contributions and closing remarks The configuration we just described allows to scale pre-training runs to 1T parameters at a workable throughput on public European infrastructure. In order to make it possible for others to reproduce these results (more details are available in a companion post ), we upstreamed all the fixes to PyTorch and TorchTitan. In addition to the three contributions we already mentioned, we contributed a shared RoPE cache to TorchTitan (2.56 GiB per GPU at our sequence length), skipping the embedding re-gather in the backward pass , and configurable seed-offset mesh axes . In PyTorch, we fixed CPU initialization resetting the RNG state and trunc_normal_ all-gathering DTensors . We also reported unattributed host memory at job start to the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, since it affects every user of the machine. Thanks to the level of control provided by PyTorch and TorchTitan, training now runs at a sustained throughput of ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200s per DDP replica, for a total of 1536 GPUs for 4 DDP replicas, and fits in memory by fully leveraging the HBM and the Grace architecture. The companion post covers the rest of the path in Figure 1: data and expert load balancing, reducing the bytes sent over InfiniBand, node-local resharding, dynamic tile scheduling in SonicMoE and capping NCCL’s SM usage. We are grateful to the European Commission for Frontier AI Grand Challenge award. We hope that this work will motivate further investments in public compute infrastructure and the continued growth of the European AI ecosystem. Learn more: Training a 1T-Parameter MoE on Jupiter (full post) PyTorch TorchTitan FlexShard Frontier AI Grand Challenge announcement

It was also designed to support scientific research at large, which led to architectural choices that are somewhat atypical in the AI space, as we’ll describe in detail later in the post. As such, reaching the 1T parameter scale while maintaining viable throughput requires careful optimizations that go beyond standard distributed techniques. In order to have access to the necessary level of flexibility to perform fine-grained optimizations to the pre-training setup, we chose to go with PyTorch and TorchTitan . Under these conditions, we raised throughput from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200 GPUs (96 nodes). We want to share the main milestones that get us there, each of which builds on TorchTitan’s design and led to contributions back to TorchTitan and PyTorch: FlexShard placement for the Muon optimizer, which removes most of the optimizer’s communication. Activation-checkpoint offloading to the Grace CPU. Running FSDP’s all-gather setup on the compute stream ( unshard_async_op ), which frees ~14 GiB of HBM per GPU. The full write-up covers the remaining changes in detail, with interactive figures and profiler traces. The machine and its constraints Each JUPITER Booster node has four NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchips. Each superchip pairs a Hopper GPU (96 GB HBM3) with a 72-core Grace CPU (120 GB LPDDR5X), connected by a 900 GB/s NVLink-C2C link. GPUs in a node are connected by NVLink 4 at 150 GB/s per direction, and each node has four InfiniBand NDR200 adapters, about 25 GB/s per GPU. Figure 2. Bandwidths within a JUPITER node, drawn to scale. All inter-node traffic leaves through the thin InfiniBand links. In addition to the accelerators, two key parts of the system are also relevant for the design: Inter-node bandwidth. InfiniBand is 36 times slower than the link between a GPU and its own CPU, and distributing a 1T parameter model over hundreds of accelerators requires crossing that boundary continuously during training. Traffic over InfiniBand must therefore aggressively overlap with computation. Host memory capacity. GH200 is available with up to 480 GB of LPDDR5X per Grace, but JUPITER’s compute nodes actually use the 120 GB configuration (as opposed to login nodes which sport 480GB), which favors bandwidth over capacity. After the kernel’s share, about 108 GiB per GPU is usable, and we found that in practice some nodes start jobs with much less. This limits how much state can be moved out of the HBM. These constraints dictate the parallelism layout: 384-way FSDP with 4-way expert parallelism inside each node and no pipeline parallelism. The MoE token all-to-all is hard to overlap, so we kept it on NVLink. Without pipeline parallelism steps tend to be shorter, which has the advantage of providing fast feedback at scale, and fixed costs are amortized via a large batch of 384 sequences of 65,536 tokens (~25M tokens per step). FSDP already provides us with the overlap of the gather of layer n+1 with the compute of layer n , so most of the remaining work goes into making the overlap effective. We achieve this across three dimensions: moving to longer sequences to compute for longer, reducing the bytes transmitted over InfiniBand, and leveraging Grace memory to provide enough total capacity to hold the model, the gradients and the optimizer state. FlexShard: Muon without the communication We use Muon for every weight matrix except the router and embeddings (about 99.5% of the parameters) and AdamW for the rest. Muon requires one fp32 state per parameter, while Adam requires two. Removing the second state is instrumental in making a 65,536-token sequence fit in memory. Muon orthogonalizes each update with a few Newton-Schulz iterations, which operate on the whole matrix. Because FSDP splits every matrix into 384 shards, a simple implementation gathers each matrix on one rank, runs Newton-Schulz there and scatters the result back. On our interconnect, this communication is too expensive. FlexShard , now part of TorchTitan, lets us control which rank owns which parameters. We shard the experts by whole expert, so every rank owns complete expert matrices and runs their Newton-Schulz iterations with no communication at all. The dense matrices, such as the attention projections, are still collected on an owning rank, and each rank processes its own experts while the dense matrices are in transit, so that communication is overlapped. With FSDP’s CPU offload, the optimizer runs on Grace, where the parameters are stored, and Newton-Schulz on 72 Arm cores takes ~35 s per step. We contributed support to TorchTitan for running Newton-Schulz on the GPU while parameters stay offloaded. The optimizer step went from 41.7 s to 2.2 s, and throughput rose from 441 to 597 tokens/s per GPU (+35%). Figure 3. Rank 0’s profiled step from 80 s onward. Top: Newton-Schulz on Grace, with the GPU idle for ~34 s after the backward pass while the CPU computes. Bottom: Newton-Schulz on Hopper, where the optimizer takes a small fraction of the step. Activation offloading to Grace The volume of weights gathered per layer does not depend on the number of tokens in our setup, so a longer sequence increases compute time while not impacting communication. We first stored activations only at layer boundaries and recomputed everything inside a layer during the backward pass. In TorchTitan this is named FullAC. Since GPU was idle for most of the baseline step, the extra compute did not lengthen it. As a result, throughput went from 90 to 370 tokens/s per GPU at 32,768 tokens. At 65,536 tokens, the boundary activations alone take 74 layers × 65,536 tokens × 6,144 × 2 bytes ≈ 55 GiB per GPU, which does not fit in HBM next to the weights. GH200 has a 900 GB/s link to 120 GB of CPU memory, so we decide to offload them. Each boundary activation is copied to Grace after the forward pass produces it, and copied back to Hopper one layer before the backward pass recomputes it. An offloading parameter sets the share of layers that offload, which trades HBM for Grace memory. TorchTitan’s activation-checkpointing wrapper made this change convenient. We contributed the hooks for activation-checkpoint offloading to TorchTitan and built our offloading strategy on top of them. With offload, throughput rose from 370 to 508 tokens/s per GPU (+37%), and the sequence length grew to 49,152 tokens and then, with Muon, to 65,536. Figure 4. Offload schedule, drawn with 16 layers in place of 74. During the forward pass, each boundary activation moves to Grace. During the backward pass, it returns to HBM one layer before its recomputation. De-fragging FSDPs Streams After an upgrade to our software stack, the CUDA caching allocator started retrying allocations on every rank at ~70% memory utilization. At the time of the retries, 25-30 GiB of HBM was free, but the allocator could not use it. After investigating the root cause, we identified it in how FSDP overlaps communication with computation. FSDP uses one compute stream and four side streams, and the allocator keeps a separate pool per stream. Memory freed by a stream can only be reused by that stream. FSDP allocates each buffer on the stream that writes it, and some of our other communication optimizations allocated temporary buffers inside FSDP’s calls, so these buffers also landed on side streams. Replaying the allocator’s event log at peak memory showed the side streams holding 27.3 GiB, of which only 6.4 GiB was in use. The remaining 20.9 GiB was out of reach of the compute stream, which then could not find a 4 GiB block for a MoE buffer. Figure 5. HBM held by each allocator stream’s cache at peak live memory, reconstructed from the allocator’s event trace on rank 0. Solid bars are live tensors, and dashed bars are cached memory that only the owning stream can reuse. Luckily, FSDP2 has a private flag, unshard_async_op , that runs the all-gather setup on the compute stream and lets NCCL run on its internal stream. The gather buffers are then allocated from, and returned to, the compute stream’s pool. We adapted our custom gather to run asynchronously, so the compute stream waits for the network only when it needs the weights. This brought the number of ranks with allocator retries from 384 to zero. Peak reserved memory went from 88.1 to 74.6 GiB, and throughput rose from 996 to 1,210 tokens/s per GPU. We proposed a TorchTitan option to enable the flag. Following the review, unshard_async_op is being moved into a public FSDP API ( PyTorch #202343 ), so other FSDP users can rely on it. Upstreaming contributions and closing remarks The configuration we just described allows to scale pre-training runs to 1T parameters at a workable throughput on public European infrastructure. In order to make it possible for others to reproduce these results (more details are available in a companion post ), we upstreamed all the fixes to PyTorch and TorchTitan. In addition to the three contributions we already mentioned, we contributed a shared RoPE cache to TorchTitan (2.56 GiB per GPU at our sequence length), skipping the embedding re-gather in the backward pass , and configurable seed-offset mesh axes . In PyTorch, we fixed CPU initialization resetting the RNG state and trunc_normal_ all-gathering DTensors . We also reported unattributed host memory at job start to the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, since it affects every user of the machine. Thanks to the level of control provided by PyTorch and TorchTitan, training now runs at a sustained throughput of ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU on 384 GH200s per DDP replica, for a total of 1536 GPUs for 4 DDP replicas, and fits in memory by fully leveraging the HBM and the Grace architecture. The companion post covers the rest of the path in Figure 1: data and expert load balancing, reducing the bytes sent over InfiniBand, node-local resharding, dynamic tile scheduling in SonicMoE and capping NCCL’s SM usage. We are grateful to the European Commission for Frontier AI Grand Challenge award. We hope that this work will motivate further investments in public compute infrastructure and the continued growth of the European AI ecosystem. items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Microsoft Research at BUILD 2026 Giving developers a hands-on look at some of the many AI-based models and tools they can use to accelerate innovation, enhance their capabilities, and quickly transform ideas into prototypes. Learn more Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.content: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 21 +15 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training. We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling ) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining. What we learned Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts: Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 17 +11 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. items.content: Back to Articles A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks. Published November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 40 +34 Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Why a voice should live on your device Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. What we released Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. Demos and first projects The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page. The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one. Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it. Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face. How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most. On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size. Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio. Inference We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®). Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself. It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs. Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer: from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) print ( f" {model.num_parameters():,} " ) # 30,788,354 print ( f" {processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,} " ) # 10,305,313 A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices . from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file path = hf_hub_download( "gradium/phonon-voices" , "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors" ) voice = load_file(path)[ "speaker_wavs" ][ 0 ].T # (num_frames, 512) The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. Models mentioned in this article 3 Datasets mentioned in this article 1 Spaces mentioned in this article 3 More Articles from our Blog audio speech leaderboard Egyptian and Nigerian English join the Open ASR Leaderboard 13 November 6, 2026 audio speech leaderboard Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning 81 September 30, 2026 Community frederik-nlp 4 days ago Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win. One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices . from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file path = hf_hub_download( "gradium/phonon-voices" , "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors" ) voice = load_file(path)[ "speaker_wavs" ][ 0 ].T # (num_frames, 512) The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win. One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting.
