For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train --config shape --latents your-username/my-meshes-trellis2 \ --push-to your-username/my-trellis2-lora --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands: export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx # Replace your-username with your Hugging Face username # For Sparse-structure Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config ss \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 # For Shape Flow DiT docker run --gpus all -- rm --shm-size 16g -e HF_TOKEN \ -v hf-cache:/root/.cache/huggingface \ -v " $PWD /work" :/workspace/work \ cr.hf.co/suvadityamuk/trellis2-finetuning-train:latest \ trellis2-train \ --config shape \ --latents suvadityamuk/gso-footwear-trellis2-latents \ --push-to your-username/trellis2-footwear-lora \ --trackio-space your-username/trellis2-trackio \ -- set max_steps=3000 i_save=500 Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso Inside the training pipeline Preprocessing into latents We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again. We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training. Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train ( ss or shape ), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning. cfg = json.load( open ( { "ss" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/ss_flow_lora_gso.json" , "shape" : "/workspace/TRELLIS.2/configs/lora/slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json" , }[FLOW] ) ) key, latents = { "ss" : ( "ss_latent" , "ss_latents/ss_enc_conv3d_16l8_fp16_64" ), "shape" : ( "shape_latent" , "shape_latents/shape_enc_next_dc_f16c32_fp16_512" ), }[FLOW] roots = json.dumps( { "gso" : { key: f" {DATA} / {latents} " , "render_cond" : f" {DATA} /renders_cond" , "meta" : DATA, } } ) ds = getattr (datasets, cfg[ "dataset" ])(roots, **cfg[ "dataset_args" ]) holdout = set ( open ( f" {DATA} /holdout.txt" ).read().split()) ds.instances = [(root, sha) for root, sha in ds.instances if sha not in holdout] batches = cycle( DataLoader( ds, batch_size=BATCH, shuffle= True , drop_last= True , num_workers= 4 , collate_fn= getattr (ds, "collate_fn" , None ), ) ) Preparing LoRA adapters We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model() . This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface. We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point ( fp32 ) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 ( bf16 ) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored. model = models.from_pretrained(cfg[ "ckpt" ]) for block in model.blocks: block.use_checkpoint = True inject_adapter_in_model( LoraConfig( r=cfg[ "rank" ], lora_alpha=cfg[ "alpha" ], target_modules=cfg[ "lora_targets" ] ), model, ) params = [] for name, p in model.named_parameters(): p.requires_grad_( "lora_" in name) if p.requires_grad: p.data = p.data. float () # fp32 master weights for LoRA params.append(p) model.cuda().train() Training It’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3 , Flux 2 , and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching. We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen. The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands. We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images. opt = torch.optim.AdamW( params, lr=cfg[ "lr" ], weight_decay=cfg[ "weight_decay" ], betas=( 0.9 , 0.95 ) ) dino = DinoV3FeatureExtractor( cfg[ "image_cond_model" ], image_size=cfg[ "image_size" ] ).cuda() We then follow these steps within the training loop: Sample a timestep t for each sample (using logitNormal for the sparse-structure flow DiT and uniform for the shape flow DiT based on the TRELLIS.2 config). Generate random noise matching the data shape and reshape t for broadcasting. Mix clean data with noise based on t (where t = 0 is data with minimal noise, and t = 1 is pure noise). Predict velocity at t × 1000 to match pretraining conditions. Calculate loss as the mean squared error between the predicted velocity and target velocity (the first derivative of x_t ). def flow_loss ( x0, cond ): s = cfg[ "t_schedule" ] t = ( torch.rand(x0.shape[ 0 ]) if s[ "name" ] == "uniform" else torch.sigmoid( torch.randn(x0.shape[ 0 ]) * s[ "args" ][ "std" ] + s[ "args" ][ "mean" ] ) ) t = t.cuda() noise = ( x0.replace(torch.randn_like(x0.feats)) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else torch.randn_like(x0) ) tv = t.view(- 1 , *[ 1 ] * ( len (x0.shape) - 1 )) x_t = ( 1 - tv) * x0 + (cfg[ "sigma_min" ] + ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * tv) * noise pred, target = model(x_t, t * 1000 , cond), ( 1 - cfg[ "sigma_min" ]) * noise - x0 return ( F.mse_loss(pred.feats, target.feats) if cfg[ "sparse" ] else F.mse_loss(pred, target) ) The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches. For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps. for step in range ( 1 , STEPS + 1 ): for _ in range (ACCUM): batch = next (batches) x0 = recursive_to_device(batch[ "x_0" ], "cuda" ) with torch.no_grad(): cond = dino(batch[ "cond" ]) cond[torch.rand( len (cond), device= "cuda" ) < cfg[ "p_uncond" ]] = 0 with torch.autocast( "cuda" , dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = flow_loss(x0, cond) / ACCUM loss.backward() torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, cfg[ "grad_clip" ]) opt.step() opt.zero_grad() Results We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours. The training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry. Flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects. The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans. We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set: Metric What it means Chamfer distance The distance from points on one surface to the nearest points on the other surface, measured in both directions. Lower is better. F-score @ 0.02 The combination of precision (how much of the generated surface is near the reference) and recall (how much of the reference surface the generated surface covers). Here, the matching threshold is 2% of the scan’s bounding-box diagonal. Higher is better. Normal consistency How closely the surface directions agree. A surface normal is a vector perpendicular to the surface. Higher is better. In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects. For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space . Future directions Phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs

items.summary:

Same change for EventuallySubset.

Deprecate some ae_le_set lemmas to ae_subset along the way.

On March 31, 2027 , the preformatted data package feature in the Data Download Program (DDP) will be retired in preparation for the July 1, 2027, DDP page removal . Users can access data and expanded download options through the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) . Learn more about the DDP and FRED partnership . The XML format is still available on Board statistical release pages for users who wish to manually download Board data from the Board's website. As of March 1, 2016, the daily effective federal funds rate (EFFR) is a volume-weighted median of transaction-level data collected from depository institutions in the Report of Selected Money Market Rates (FR 2420). Prior to March 1, 2016, the EFFR was a volume-weighted mean of rates on brokered trades. 2. Weekly figures are averages of 7 calendar days ending on Wednesday of the current week; monthly figures include each calendar day in the month. 3. Annualized using a 360-day year or bank interest. 4. On a discount basis. 5. Interest rates interpolated from data on certain commercial paper trades settled by The Depository Trust Company. The trades represent sales of commercial paper by dealers or direct issuers to investors (that is, the offer side). The 1-, 2-, and 3-month rates are equivalent to the 30-, 60-, and 90-day dates reported on the Board's Commercial Paper Web page ( www.federalreserve.gov/releases/cp/ ). 6. Financial paper that is insured by the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program is not excluded from relevant indexes, nor is any financial or nonfinancial commercial paper that may be directly or indirectly affected by one or more of the Federal Reserve's liquidity facilities. Thus the rates published after September 19, 2008, likely reflect the direct or indirect effects of the new temporary programs and, accordingly, likely are not comparable for some purposes to rates published prior to that period. 7. Rate posted by a majority of top 25 (by assets in domestic offices) insured U.S.-chartered commercial banks. Prime is one of several base rates used by banks to price short-term business loans. 8. The rate charged for discounts made and advances extended under the Federal Reserve's primary credit discount window program, which became effective January 9, 2003. This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . The rate reported is that for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Historical series for the rate on adjustment credit as well as the rate on primary credit are available at www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/data.htm . 9. Yields on actively traded non-inflation-indexed issues adjusted to constant maturities. The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: November 12, 2026 Back to Top

items.title: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
items.summary: Andrea is a Senior Developer Advocate at GitHub with over a decade of experience in developer tools. She combines technical depth with a mission to make advanced technologies more accessible. After transitioning from Army service and construction management to software development, she brings a unique perspective to bridging complex engineering concepts with practical implementation. She lives in Florida with her Welsh partner, two sons, and two dogs, where she continues to drive innovation and support open source through GitHub's global initiatives. Find her online @acolombiadev.
